segments.say: There's a kind of waiting that's different from all the others. Waiting for news that matters. You've taken an exam, and the results won't be out for weeks. You've applied for a job you really want. You've had a medical test, and the doctor will call. The outcome is already decided, in a way. You just don't know it yet.

This kind of waiting has a special flavor. You can't do anything to change the outcome anymore. The exam is written. The application is sent. And yet your mind keeps returning to it. What if it's bad? What if it's good? You rehearse both possibilities, over and over, in the quiet moments of the day.

show.cap: The answer is already out there

segments.say: Kate Sweeny, a psychologist at the University of California, Riverside, has spent years studying exactly this. She calls it waiting for uncertain news. And she's looked at people in real situations. Law students waiting for their bar exam results, which decide whether they can work as lawyers. Doctoral students waiting to hear about job applications. People waiting for medical results.

Her research and that of others has found that this kind of waiting can be really stressful. Worry tends to rise and fall during the wait. And it often goes up again just before the news arrives. The final days, or hours, can be the hardest. Many people describe the last moments before opening an email, or answering a call, as almost unbearable.

Sweeny and her colleagues have also studied something many of us do without thinking. Bracing. As the moment of truth approaches, people often lower their expectations. They start to prepare for bad news, even if they were optimistic before. It's a kind of emotional protection. If the news is bad, it won't hurt so much. If it's good, it will feel like a pleasant surprise.

And here's an interesting finding from her work. Worrying during the wait doesn't feel good, of course. But some of her research suggested that people who worried more during the wait sometimes felt relatively better when the news came, whether the news was good or bad. Bad news felt less of a shock. Good news felt like a bigger relief.

That doesn't mean worry is good. Spending weeks consumed by anxiety is exhausting, and it takes away from everything else in life. So the question becomes, how can we wait for important news without being swallowed by it? And one of Sweeny's most interesting answers involves a famous video game.

In one study, two hundred and ninety students were told that other people were rating how attractive they were. While they waited for these ratings, they played Tetris for ten minutes. Some played at an easy level, which was boring. Some at a very hard level, which was overwhelming. And some at an adaptive level, which got harder as they got better.

show.who: Kyla Rankin, Lilly Walsh & Kate Sweeny
show.where: University of California, Riverside, published in Emotion, 2019
show.what: 290 students were told they were being rated by others, and waited for the results while playing Tetris at easy, adaptive or very hard levels for 10 minutes.

segments.say: The adaptive level was designed to create something psychologists call flow. That wonderful state where you're so absorbed in an activity that you lose track of time. It happens when something is challenging enough to hold your attention, but not so hard that you feel overwhelmed. Just right.

And the people who played at the adaptive level, the ones most likely to get into flow, reported less negative emotion and more positive emotion than those who were bored or overwhelmed. In the studies with the law students and the doctoral students, more flow during the waiting period was also linked to less worry.

What's interesting is that it's not just about distraction. Easy Tetris was a distraction too, but it was boring, so the mind could still wander back to the worry. Very hard Tetris was frustrating. What helped most was being truly absorbed. An activity that fills your mind so completely that there's no room left for worry.

Flow can come from many things. Cooking a new recipe. Playing music. A puzzle. A sport. Gardening. Drawing. A good conversation. Even some kinds of work. The key is that it should be engaging, a bit challenging, and something you can lose yourself in. If you're facing a long wait for news, planning some flow activities could be a kind gift to yourself.

And if you're waiting for something important right now, I want to say, gently, that it's okay to find it hard. Waiting for news that matters is one of the most challenging experiences in life. It's normal to worry, to check, to imagine. You're not doing it wrong. Be as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend in the same situation.

So here's what research on waiting for news suggests. Worry often rises just before the news arrives. As the moment approaches, we brace ourselves by lowering expectations. Flow, being fully absorbed in something, can ease the worry. And absorbing activities seem to help more than simple distraction.

show.title: Waiting for news, gently
items: Worry often rises just before the news
Flow can ease worry during the wait

segments.say: So far, we've talked about waits we'd rather avoid. But now I'd like to turn things around. Because there's a kind of waiting that people actually enjoy. Sometimes, they even choose to wait longer, just to savor it. An economist once asked people about a kiss from a film star, and discovered something delightful.
